n: Reuben was Jacob’s firstborn, but he lost the birthright after sleeping with his father’s concubine. The double inheritance of the firstborn went to Joseph’s sons instead.

f.w: his birthright was given unto the sons of Joseph

n: The chronicler explains a key distinction: Judah became the royal tribe that produced kings, but the birthright belonged to Joseph. Both roles matter in God’s plan for Israel.

f.w: of him came the chief ruler

n: Reuben’s four sons, founders of Reubenite clans, are named.

f.w: Hanoch, and Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi

n: A line of Reubenite descendants through Joel, whose link to Reuben’s sons is not given.

f.g: A Reubenite; not the Gog of Ezekiel’s prophecy (Ezekiel 38).

n: The line continues; one descendant is even named Baal, a sign of Canaanite influence in the family.

f.g: “Lord” or “master”—also the name of the Canaanite storm god.

n: Beerah, a Reubenite chief, was taken captive by Assyria’s King Tiglath-pileser III around 732 BC.

f.g: Tiglath-pileser III, king of Assyria about 745–727 BC.

n: Other Reubenite clan leaders are listed according to the official family records.

f.w: the genealogy of their generations was reckoned
f.g: When the family records were officially recorded.

n: Bela’s clan lived around Aroer, Nebo and Baal-meon, towns east of the Dead Sea in the former lands of Sihon.
Their herds grew so large that they spread east toward the desert stretching to the Euphrates.

f.g: The fertile highlands east of the Jordan River.

n: In Saul’s day the Reubenites defeated the Hagarites, a nomadic people, and took over their land.

f.g: Desert nomads, possibly linked by name with Hagar, mother of Ishmael.

n: The tribe of Gad lived north of Reuben in Bashan, a region famous for its rich pasture and strong cattle.

f.g: A fertile plateau east of the Sea of Galilee.

n: The chief leaders of Gad are listed.

f.g: The leading clan head of Gad.

n: Seven more Gadite family heads.

f.g: The chronicler often totals names to aid memory and accuracy.

n: Their ancestry is traced back many generations to Buz.

f.g: Here a personal name, the same as the region.

n: Ahi was head of this Gadite family group.

f.w: chief of the house of their fathers
f.g: Head of the extended family or clan.

n: Gad lived in Gilead, Bashan and the pasturelands of a region called Sharon east of the Jordan.

f.g: Not the coastal plain of Sharon but an area east of the Jordan with the same name.
Pasturelands around towns.

n: These records were compiled in the eighth century BC, under Jotham of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel—shortly before the northern tribes were exiled.

f.g: Jeroboam II (about 793–753 BC).

n: The tribes east of the Jordan fielded an army of 44,760 trained warriors.

f.g: A small round shield.

n: They fought the Hagarites and their allies, desert tribes descended from Ishmael.
This is a key verse for the chronicler’s message: they won because they cried to God in battle and trusted Him. Faith, not military strength, brings victory.

f.w: they cried to God in the battle

f.g: He listened to their plea and answered it.

n: They captured enormous herds and many captives. The large numbers emphasize how complete the victory was.

f.g: Donkeys.

n: The battle was “of God,” so the victory was great. Yet the verse ends ominously: they lived there only until the captivity.

f.g: In their place.

n: The eastern half-tribe of Manasseh grew and spread north to Mount Hermon.

f.g: The Amorite name for Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9).

n: Manasseh’s leaders are praised as mighty and famous men.

f.g: Strong, brave warriors—also used for men of wealth and standing.

n: But they turned away from God to worship the gods of the land. Their earlier trust in God gave way to unfaithfulness.

f.g: A strong biblical image: idolatry as unfaithfulness in a marriage covenant with God.

n: God allowed the Assyrian kings to carry these tribes into exile around 732 BC. These became part of the scattered “lost tribes,” whose gathering the restored Church teaches will be part of the latter days.

f.g: Pul is another name for Tiglath-pileser III; the verse names the same king twice.
